Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to second the motion of the Prime Minister. In doing so I might say that I observed in the proceedings this morning that there was no
word of greeting to His Excellency in the French language. In view of the fact that under the British North America Act we have two official languages in this house, I should like to suggest that these proceedings be printed in both languages.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

speechtext:
May I say to my hon. friend and to the house that on these matters precedent is followed. All arrangements are made by a committee, of which the chairman usually is the Under-Secretary of State. I have asked Mr. Coleman with respect to the proceedings and he has given me a memorandum in which he says that he had carefully looked into the matter before the arrangements were made and that the records in the department indicate that previous governors general have said a few words in French only on occasions when the installation took place at Quebec. On those occasions addresses of welcome were presented on behalf of the city and tne province, which were in French, and normally the Governor General replied to these by speaking briefly in that language. In the case of Lord Tweedsmuir this occurred. In the case of the Earl of Athlone, who was sworn in in the senate chamber, and the Earl of Bessborough, who was sworn in at Halifax, their addresses in reply were entirely in English. From the above it would appear that the proceedings of this morning were in accordance with precedent.
Of course I am only too prepared to take the responsibility for all the proceedings, and, in particular for the address of welcome having been presented only in English this morning, but I can assure my hon. friend that there was no discourtesy intended either to His Excellency the Governor General or to our friends from the province of Quebec or any other part of' Canada.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the widespread public discussion at the present time with regard to UNRRA, I thought that the house might be interested in having a brief report regarding the Canadian contribution to UNRRA.
Canada's total contribution to UNRRA up to March 31, 1946, was $154,000,000. Of this amount, ten per cent has been reserved as UNRRA free funds expendable in any part of the world. The balance reserved for expenditure in Canada is, therefore, $138,600,000. As of March 31 of this year, $119,000,000 has been committed by various government departments and agencies leaving approximately $19,000,000 uncommitted, of which it is estimated that ten per cent should be removed for freight storage and handling charges. The exact figure of the balance available for future purchases on March 31 was $17,350,532.87.
Hon. members will be interested to know in greater detail how this $119,000,000 has been committed. A sum of $27,500,000 has been set aside for the purchase of wheat and grain; $16,000,000 for meat and more than $2,500,000 for seeds and milk. The grain has been purchased by the wheat and grain division of this department, and the seeds, meat and milk by the Department of Agriculture. The Department of Munitions and Supply has contracted for $2,300,000 worth of electrical equipment. The Canadian Export Board have made commitments on behalf of UNRRA for $56,500,000 worth of goods under the following headings:

REVOCATION OP ORDER IN COUNCIL P.C. 4671
speechtext:
I wish to announce that order in council P.C. 4671 of the 7th June, 1943, was revoked to-day. This order provided that the only statutory holidays which "should be observed by employers and employees" during the war were to be New Year's day, Good Friday, Dominion day, Labour day, Thanksgiving day and Christmas day. The same order similarly restricted the number of statutory holidays to be observed by the public service of Canada and those which were during the period indicated to be legal holidays or non-juridical days within the meaning of the Bills of Exchange Act.
As a result of the action now taken, the definition of "holiday" in the Interpretation Act is again in full effect. The holidays to be observed by the public service are again those enumerated in section 45 of the Civil Service Act, and again are those to be observed as legal holidays or non-juridical days. The result will be that, among others, Easter Monday and Victoria day will be observed as statutory holidays this year.
With regard to Remembrance day, the Minister of Veterans Affairs in particular has been in consultation with the national veterans organizations of the country. It seems desirable that before a definite decision with regard to that day be made, full consultation with veterans organizations should be proceeded with. Some of these organizations are holding annual meetings-one, early in May- and as soon as the veterans have had an opportunity of conferring further with the Minister of Veterans Affairs, in particular, a definite policy with regard to that day and,
I may say, a definite decision with regard to holidays generally other than those covered by the present announcement, will be made.

subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATIVES IN TRIALS AT HONG KONG

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATIVES IN TRIALS AT HONG KONG
speechtext:
The hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) asked me a question yesterday and I said I would give a reply to-day. The question was whether a Canadian representative has been appointed for the trials of Japanese war criminals at Hong Kong which are now proceeding, and when the representative will be dispatched.
In order that hon. members may get a true perspective of the whole matter as it arises out of the question which has been asked by the hon. member, I will give the house a brief review of the arrangements which have been concluded with regard to Canadian participation in the trials of far eastern war criminals generally.
The major war criminals are to be tried by an international tribunal, convened by General MacArthur, to which each state signatory to the Japanese surrender instrument has been invited to name a judge and an associate prosecutor. The Canadian nominee as judge is Mr. Justice E. Stuart McDougall, of the Court of King's Bench, Quebec, and the Canadian nominee as associate prosecutor is Brigadier H. G. Nolan,- C.B.E., M.C., Vice-Judge Advocate General at national defence headquarters. Both Brigadier Nolan and Judge McDougall have been in Tokyo since February.
Canadian participation in the trials of the lesser far eastern war criminals has been complicated by the fact that under existing international arrangements military courts for the trial of such war criminals may only be convened by states now in occupation of areas formerly dominated by Japan. Moreover, under the war crimes regulations (Canada), Canadian military courts can only be convened by senior officers in command of "Canadian forces"; since Canada has had no occupation force in the far east, no such courts could be convened in that area.
However, arrangements have been concluded with the governments of the United Kingdom and the United States pursuant to 63260-52
which a group of Canadian officers are proceeding to Hong Kong and Tokyo to exercise the following powers and duties:
(a)	to assist in the collection and collation of further evidence of atrocities against Canadians;
(b)	to assist in providing the United Kingdom (or United States) authorities with such available evidence from Canadian sources as may be considered of value to them;
(c)	to request the United Kingdom (or United States) military authorities to convene military courts under their respective war crimes regulations for the trial of particular persons within their jurisdiction against whom, in the opinion of the appropriate Canadian military representative, a prima facie case of a war crime against a Canadian has been established;
(d)	to assist in the prosecution of Canadian cases if so authorized by the appropriate United Kingdom (or United States) military authority;
(e)	to act in general liaison with the United Kingdom (or United States) war crimes officers in the far east.
In implementation of these arrangements, four Canadian army officers and four other ranks, with Lieutenant Colonel J. O. H. Orr in charge, are now en route to the far east. These officers will act in both the Hong Kong and Tokyo areas. The officers, all of whom possess legal experience, were drawn largely from the war crimes section at national defence headquarters; two of the other ranks are ex-Hong Kong prisoners of war.
Evidence of far eastern crimes against Canadian citizens and members of the Canadian armed forces has been collected and collated by a war crimes -section at national defence headquarters. The section has reported that there is an accumulation of evidence of atrocities against Canadians both in the areas now occupied by the United Kingdom forces (that is, Hong Kong) and in Japan proper.
Lists and descriptions of "wanted" persons have been transmitted to the appropriate United Kingdom and United States authorities with the request that they be apprehended, or held in cusody if already apprehended.
The war crimes officers en route to the far east have with them the evidence above referred to and will keep in close touch with the war crimes section at national defence headquarters.	<
The United States authorities have requested that an additional officer accompany the officers proceeding to Tokyo and be available to sit as judge on any joint military court convened by General MacArthur for the trial of lesser war criminals whether the victims were

Canadians or nationals of other countries. Colonel Thomas Moss, M.C., K.C., of the Judge Advocate General's branch, has been assigned for this purpose and has now left Ottawa en route to Tokyo. It may also be that conversations held by the war crimes officers in Hong Kong will indicate that it would be in order for a judicial officer to be sent to Hong Kong to carry out similar functions.

I am compelled to admit that international isolationism will in future be a monstrous utopia, and |hat the Canadian people who have emerged from the crucible of war bruised but grown in stature, must comply, like any other entity living under the sun, with the unyielding laws that govern the progress towards maturity. The proposal must therefore be examined from the standpoint of national interest. And that is what I have tried to do.
Canadians will enjoy prosperity only if they have an adequate income. Therefore, if the national income is maintained on a high level, our entire nation will be prosperous. The shrinking and freezing of capital are the source of economic depressions. Our experiences from 1930 to 1935 should not be soon forgotten. In order to maintain the national income at a high level, it is necessary that the purchasing power in the hands of the taxpayer be also on a high level to enable him to meet taxation and high prices. In other words, it is essential to have a sound monetary unit in free circulation, creating profits and prosperity. Eisler in his book entitled "Stable Money", pages 16 and 17, reviews the situation as follows:
(Text):
The purchasing power of the consumer is obviously measured by the total amount of cash and credit available to him for spending at any moment on goods and services for immediate consumption. As the monetary unit will buy a varying quantity of goods according to whether the average price of goods-the so-called "general price level"-is high or low, the consumers' real capacity for acquiring goods will be measured by the sum total of their nominal monetary incomings for a given period, minus their savings, multiplied by the reciprocal value of the index of retail prices, i.e., by the purchase power of the monetary unit.
If goods are to flow steadily from the producer to the ultimate consumer, the real purchasing power of the consumer must be equivalent to the total money value of the goods destined for immediate consumption offered by the producers during the same period. And this state of affairs may be described as the ideal or normal equilibrium of the national or world market.	.
Should the consumers' purchasing power . . . be greater at a given period than the capacity of industry and agriculture to produce directly consumable goods, prices will rise and the owners of capital will be spurred by the prospect of profit to increasing their producing capacity by installing new machinery and by engaging more labour, thereby further increasing the purchasing power of the consumers. If, however, the sum total of money available for spending on commodities is less than the total money value of sucli goods offered by their producers, prices will fall.
production will be reduced and producers will refrain from increasing their plant or staff, thus further restricting the consumers' purchasing power. Consequently the situation on the market for producers' goods is always entirely dependent on the situation on th'e market for consumers' goods. Both markets must stagnate and employment of every kind must shrink if too little money flows to the second of the two.

And have we heard protests from the hon. members who are opposed to the resolution? No, Mr. Speaker. Such silence is sufficient proof of their intentions. You may draw your own conclusions.
I hope that by causing money to circulate a lot more in our country, the loan will create employment to the benefit of all classes. Manufacturing for export will create employment and I wonder if the government's critics on this score can afford to shoulder the tremendous responsibility of refusing their support to a bill which may create more jobs, simply, in some cases, because of political anglophobia? Can they suggest a better way of solving unemployment, which is getting more acute every day? I would gladly hear them put forward some constructive suggestion instead of their destructive criticisms. Public administration in Canada would benefit by such a display of true Canadianism.
Some critics contend that the loan is further proof of our British colonialism. I would not go that far. Our neighbours to the south have lent nearly 5 billions on similar terms, and yet we could hardly accuse them of British colonialism. Our loans to Prance and Belgium did1 not mean that we are their colony. I say rather that Canada must pay to reconquer her foreign markets and that Great Britain is one market we cannot afford to lose. Everyone knows that colonial ties still bind Canada to Great Britain; Westminster has not yet accomplished the miracle of granting us complete independence. At least, that is my personal opinion. But to come 'to the conclusion that any financial transaction between Canada and England constitutes a gesture of colonial dependency seems somewhat radical. We might discuss at great length the methods resorted to by the British to restore their economy. We are all entitled to our own opinions
on the matter; however, the fact remains that Canada must have access to the world markets and accept such satisfactory compromises as are required in the gigantic struggle which is actually being waged in our confused world.
Those remarks will explain clearly my stand in regard to the loan to England. I have examined the facts purely from the standpoint of a business transaction leaving sentimentality out of the picture.
I trust that those remarks will not offend anyone; I have made them in good faith and in a spirit of fairness. I am sure that this loan to England, will be approved by a great majority of the Canadian people, for the war has taught us a grim lesson and has convinced us that isolationism is out of the question, that the trend of world's public opinion cannot be disregarded and that we, in Canada, must go hand in hand with the great trading nations of the world. This entails obligations, Mr. Speaker, and I am convinced that the house is fully aware of that, but we must not shirk our national obligations and it is the bounden duty of each, and everyone of us to endorse proposals which now or later will provide our workers with jobs and with an adequate income.
It is in that spirit, Mr. Speaker, that I will approve the loan unreservedly, leaving it to the government to carry out those proposals and to my constituents to pass judgment upon me at the opportune moment. Indeed, during the last federal election, my constituents were of the opinion that the policy of the present government in such matters is a sound one, for as stated by the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Belzile) yesterday, the campaign in the constituency of Labelle as well as in his own riding hinged upon the gifts or loans to England. I had supported such gifts or loans at the time and I support the present loan, for I am convinced that the, constituency of Labelle, as all the other constituencies of the country, will derive benefits from this sound legislation.

I know some seasonal workers, such as stevedores, lumbermen, railway employees, who would be pleased to enjoy unemployment benefits, either non-existent or inadequate at the present time; an improvement in the condition-of these people who comprise the greatest part of our population would increase the general well-being of Canada in permitting a greater expansion of our wealth and a fairer distribution of our public funds.
Since I have had the privilege of holding a seat in this house, I have heard almost daily, hon. members making various requests: for the building of a railway line or a seaport, for an increase in the old age pension or the pension to the blind. One would request that researches for a cancer cure be not hindered by the lack of necessary funds; another, that a benefit system be inaugurated for the crippled without income or revenue; and there are also the requests for bridges, post offices and other public buildings. Another member would ask air mail for his district. Hardly a speech that does not refer to an old or a new request
Should we not, Mr. Speaker, first grant all reasonable requests, either by lending the amount required or granting the sums asked for, before giving additional millions of dollars to an Empire whose wealth is incredible? What we want for Canada, is a sane legislation and a conservative financial management; this is more important than entering the international race with millions and billions of dollars. All the arguments advanced or to be advanced in favour of the agreement between Canada and Great Britain which is submitted to us at the present time, do not and will not alter the fact that when one has not enough money to meet his obligations, one is ill-advised to make additional debts in order to make a loan to one's neighbour.
"A deep and prevailing national feeling is not a luxury for Canada, it is a necessity", such were the words used in 1939, by the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), and this is why I am willing to vote billions of dollars for the care, protection and future welfare of my Canadian fellow-citizens, while refusing to support this agreement. As the hon. member for Gharlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion) stated, on March 26 last:
Before paying millions every year on account of the loan made to another country, our leaders should show the people that they are ready to undertake the public works which are sorely needed.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few remarks on the measure now under consideration. The tax-paying public does not seem to welcome as readily as do some hon. members of this house the idea of lending $1,250 million to England. I should like to indicate some of the reasons why I feel bound to oppose this measure which, to my mind, borders on extravagance.
My opposition comes, in the first place, from the instructions of my constituents. I have received numerous protests from my electors. I have made a personal investigation and I must say that I have not met one person, of whatever political party, to whom such an utter prodigality has not been a cause of deep resentment.
If the	hon. members of this house
are still the representatives of the people, rather than the tools of a dictatorship, I believe that the opinion of my constituents must influence the stand we have to take on this matter.
I am not against this proposal merely because of the views of my electors, I oppose it on behalf of the 150,000 voters who, in the last election, accepted, as their own the Bloc Populaire's motto "Canada for Canadians". Now, so that no one may'charge me with being an isolationist, I should like to refer to the views that have been voiced throughout the province by prominent journalists and people who are outstanding in the field of economic and political science in our province. Here is what the brilliant parliamentary correspondent of L'Action Catholique had to say in an outspoken article published on March 9, 1946:
It is true that our gifts for this week give us a respite of a couple of years and that they will maintain our economic activity during that limited period. This dubious result is obtained by unnatural means, just as the spark of life is sustained in a dying man through the administration of a drug.
The same writer, had this to say in the same paper on March 12, 1946:
The naked truth is that Greit Britain will in future receive our products and distribute them in order to maintain her trade and her imperial policy, and that the Canadians will have to foot the bill.
I must recall to the house that L'Action Catholique has a circulation of 80.000 to
80,000	in the province of Quebec. The outspoken opinion of that parliamentary correspondent is fully confirmed by experts. I am referring to Mr. Roger Yezina, editor of the financial page in L'Action Catholique, who in the April 2, 1946 issue of that paper expressed the following opinion:

For the future, the loan may therefore result in a decrease of Canada's exports to England.
Let me refer to the following statement made by the Minister of Finance:
In other words Canada (the creditor nation) must increase her imports in order to be paid.

But if things keep i-n the trend of the past six years, Mr. Usley will be proven wrong and history will show that no country, in the experience the world, has evinced Canada's gullibility in agreeing blindly to sacrifice the interests ot her producers to those of another nation, England in this case, for the sole purpose of helping that country to squeeze her out of the international market.

Any reasons or pretexts brought up in favour of new financial sacrifices to the cause of imperialism will not alter the fact that these sacrifices go beyond what can be expected of Canadian democracy.

We need not hesitate to censure the abuse of power instanced by this advance of $1,250,000,000 to Great Britain without the previous approval of parliament whose great mistake was to give a free hand to the executive.

That in the opinion of this house the federal parliament should decline to implement the projected financial agreement between Great Britain and Canada, unless the dominion government establish that this agreement is beneficial from a Canadian point of view.

Mr. Speaker, I had hoped there would be a degree of unanimity on this important bill. It did seem to me that those who are charged with the responsibility of viewing the important features of this loan must have given it a great deal of consideration; and for the psychological effect it would have seemed to be in order for us to accept the report of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) and give this loan early approval, since indeed it will have much to do with our future prosperity.
The hon. gentleman who preceded me (Mr. Dionne) spoke of Britain driving a hard bargain. Well, there was a time when her bargaining powers were limited; but we who

indeed were her debtors morally were willing [DOT] to accept her decision in the greatest game ever played on an international scale, during the tragic war just concluded. So that for a few moments, if I may, I wish to direct your attention to Britain's position in the days before the war and trace something of the contribution and the tremendous sacrifices she made during that trying period. I do not intend to refer to her bravery or sacrifices on the field of battle, but rather to her economic sacrifices, to her position in world affairs which she was prepared to risk in order to stand forth as the stalwart defender of freedom and civilization.
Annually before the war Britain bought more goods of every kind than any other single country in the world. That is a fact which should not be lost sight of, inasmuch as it indicates the key position she occupied; and I believe world economists recognize to-day that unless she is able to regain some semblance of that position the recovery we are all so anxious to bring about may be hampered. Not only was Britain a large importer of goods; she was also a great exporter. One-fifth of the world's foreign commerce moved through Britain's ports, So that when we think of the position Britain occupied in trading with the whole world, we cannot avoid gaining some conception of how important it will be for us to seek to channel commerce and trade through the same ports which have served the world so well in the past.
What is the position to-daj^? What is known as the sterling bloc accounts for almost one-third of the world's trade. Britain now is indebted to this sterling bloc for goods received during the war to the extent of
814.000	million. If we try a squeeze play, if I might use that term, we may drive Britain to trade within this sterling bloc, to which she will be bound to export her goods in order to satisfy her creditors; and while this huge volume of trade is going on we in the dollar bloc will suffer most. As a matter of fact, in my opinion it would be nothing short of a tragedy were we to allow a competitive situation to develop between these two great trading blocs. The hon. gentleman who preceded me mentioned the hard bargain that Britain drove. Well, when it comes to surviving the bargain would be harder still, because Britain and the whole sterling bloc would be pitted against the dollar bloc and fighting for survival in the most tragic economic war one could possibly imagine.
During the war Britain cut her exports by more than sixty-six per cent, in her all-out effort to stem the tide. Her whole epergy,

Loan to United Kingdom
every fibre and force of her being, was directed in one course. It was to bring about some degree of security to determine that an ideology which had no place among freedom loving people would not gain a dominant position in world affairs.
I come now to the purpose of this loan. As I understand it, this loan has a direct relationship to the loan now pending approval in the United States of America. The best authorities there indicate that the object is to stabilize currency. It is said that with this credit and the credit which will be passed by Washington there will exist a dollar exchange so that this country, whether trading in a sterling area or in a dollar area, will have funds which will be readily convertible into dollars or pounds sterling. It seems to me that this is a move in the right direction which we have sought to make for many long years.
Most people agree that there must be a lowering of tariff barriers, or trade barriers if you will. You are not going to accomplish your purpose if you set up a barrier more difficult to hurdle, a barrier of currency which cannot be exchanged into funds which are acceptable in our own country. I can visualize a tremendous volume of trade from this one and a quarter billion dollar loan which we would otherwise lose. I do not think there is any doubt about that in the minds of those who are present to-day.
We should not charge Britain with being a hard customer to deal with. I think we can adopt a rather selfish attitude with respect to this loan inasmuch as Canada will stand to benefit from it just as much if not more than Great Britain. As a matter of fact, without this loan our agricultural industry and hundreds of our workshops might *have to shut down. If you can visualize the situation resulting from a condition of that nature then I think you will agree that the loan means as much to us as it does to Great Britain. When in the days of the war it was necessary to supply Britain with ammunition and implements of warfare, guns, ships and so on, we never hesitated. We furnished those things which were needed solely for destruction.
It has been said that probably Britain will turn around and lend money to other nations in Europe. I would have no objection to that. I do not think we should seek to follow through. If we supply goods to Britain and she in turn can pass them on to others who are in need, having arranged the necessary credits or exchange, that would seem to me to be good business. It would
be setting up the scheme which we are seeking so hard to set up, world trade, trade throughout the civilized world.
When we read the press comments on the situation in Europe we realize that Europe is on the verge of starvation; Not many people in this country know what it means to be without food, without the necessary nourishment to keep body and soul together. Food is the one thing that probably will save Europe from anarchy or revolution. If the people there face starvation, if their calorific intake is' not sufficient to maintain them, the result will be that disease will run rampant, tuberculosis and other tragedies will wait upon the human race.
If we are to bring about a better world it would seem that this will be achieved through the channels of trade. I have said before that we come to know better the people with whom we do business than we do strangers. This is our opportunity to play our part at an important moment in world history. I doubt if many of us realize just how serious the situation is. Without this loan and the loan now pending approval in the United States we do not know what forces will come into being, seeking in a competitive way, in a hard, cold, clear way, to gain dominance in world trade.
I recall Britain's position after the war. She found herself hopelessly indebted, both in the sterling bloc and in the dollar bloc. The dollar bloc countries have realized already the importance of maintaining Britain's trade position. I think it must be admitted that Britain is the one nation in the world which has been proved in the past to represent the frontier of democratic civilization. We must endeavour to protect our great ally who during the war years was willing to sacrifice all her foreign investments. No sacrifice was too great for her to make, and her foreign investments were sold in order to create credit with which she could purchase the necessary instruments and implements for war.
I hope we do not delay too long in coming to a decision, in making up our minds that this is possibly one of the most important bills to come before the House of Commons. I leave my hon. friends who will follow me with this thought: This is our opportunity to endorse what has been said by others who

Mr. Speaker, in speaking to the principle of this bill I think I shall take my cue from the last member who spoke and make my remarks brief so that we can expedite the business of the house. I expected that this debate would take two or three weeks,, but I heard over the grapevine that it would be wound up before the recess at Easter. For that reason I have to get in on the debate quite early.
The bill we have before us contains more than one principle. One principle is that a large sum of money owed by Great Britain to Canada shall be cancelled. Some hon. members have referred to that as a gift. To me a gift is something that we give now or in the future, whereas this is a debt that was incurred in the past and we are now cancelling it. I am glad that we- are cancelling it.
However, when I think of the amount of this cancellation that we are making to the people of Great Britain I also think of some of the debts and hardships facing certain people of Canada. I have in mind our old age pensioners. It would be a fine gesture on our part if we could see to it that the caveats are removed from the homes and properties of people who receive old age pensions. There are people in Canada, home owners and , farmers, who have secured debts against their properties. Some of those debts have been attached to those properties for twenty or thirty years, and I think this government would be supported in any measure they would bring forward, to cancel those particular debts, and as well the 817,000,000 odd which the soldier settlers of the first great war owe under the Soldier Settlement Act. At this time when we are cancelling $425,000,000 of a debt that is owed to us by Great Britain this government should certainly be able to cancel the $17,000,000 that is owed by the soldier settlers.
Another principle in this bill is that for a number of years the loan shall be interest-free, and after that the rate of interest shall be low. That, too, I think is a very good principle. It is a principle that we have seen developing in

Canada over the past twenty years. The government bonds floated in the first great war paid five per cent interest. Most of the bonds floated by the government in this war paid three per cent interest. The banks used to charge eight and nine per cent interest on loans; they now charge six per cent. I think that is a good thing. I am opposed to interest at any tirhe on anything beyond the amount of interest that is necessary to cover the charges of making the transaction and carrying the debt. It was a revelation in irony to see on the same order paper on which the resolution appeared for cancelling the debt to Great Britain another resolution reducing the rate of interest which the soldier settlers of the first great war have to pay on their debt to three and a half per cent. We are at tins time making a loan to Britain that will carry two per cent interest. Yet at the same time we are asking that the Canadian veterans of the first great war pay three and a half per cent interest, or 150 per cent more interest than we are asking the people of Great Britain to pay. Surely we do not love the people of Great Britain more than we love our own veterans. I suggest that the veterans of both wars be given interest rates not greater in any event than two per cent. I think also that the interest rate charged by the farm loan board might be reduced from five to two per cent and that bank loan interest should be reduced to two per cent. We should take our action on this loan to Great Britain as a criterion of the amount of interest that shall be charged on loans to Canadians. I am opposed to Canadian workers, farmers and small business men paying more than two per cent interest on any type of debt.
We, in this group should examine this proposition, if possible from the point of view of orthodox financial policy. I regret very much that I have not with me a statement to which I can refer closely as did the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) in the address that he delivered yeserday, and I shall have to attempt to get along by referring to a few heads.
In the past the people of Canada believed and to-day they are being told by people in many quarters that for Canada to prosper we must have large amounts of exports; more than that, that we must have an excess of exports over imports, and to the extent that we have that excess of export over imports we shall have prosperity at home. The argument is a fallacy, but in some ways it worked pretty well in practice under the present economic set-up. If we have an excess of exports over imports the Canadian producers of those exports are not

Loan to United Kingdom
getting pound sterling or United States dollars for what they produce, but are getting Canadian dollars and deposits in Canadian banks, and because they have those deposits they are able to purchase the things they need. If we are to follow the argument, which I do not agree with, that prosperity in Canada depends on a large export trade over our imports, the government would have been wise in the interests of this system to make this whole loan a gift, because then they would not have to be faced, as they surely will be faced, with the difficulty of having imports come to Canada in large quantities to pay for the loan.
I believe that Britain will pay back or will be prepared to pay back the amount of this loan. We shall be making from now until 1951 a loan to Great Britain of $1,250,000,000, which is a capital export. After 1951 Great Britain will start, to pay back that loan and then there will be an import of capital into Canada, which will accompany the import of goods.
From 1919 to 1928 Canada on the average exported annually capital amounts of from $500,000,000 to $700,000,000 and we had prosperity. We were exporting more than we were importing. We were exporting goods much of which no doubt we could have consumed, but we had prosperity. The years 1929, 1930 and 1931 saw capital exports and capital imports almost balance, and then we had a severe depression on our hands. If, when Great Britain is paying back this loan, we are not able to find other investments for Canadian money, we shall not have a large export of capital and we shall again, I am certain, be faced with a depression.
This loan is different from other investments in that it is made to a government. I believe that the day is past when financial interests in Canada or the United States could invest their money in the natural resources of any country to exploit the people of that country, and the government of every nation in the world is going to watch very carefully in future the amount of foreign capital that is being sent into the country. So that, if we want to export our capital we shall have to do so through government bodies. I do not think governments of other nations will be prepared after a few years to accept our capital exports, and I do not think the people of Canada will be prepared to give them. Therefore, if we are to accept payment for this loan we shall have to import more goods than we are exporting. If we attempt to import more goods than we export I can foresee that a great howl will be set up in Canada by all the financial interests, monopolies and cartels, and thev no doubt will have
an even greater effect in the future than they have had in the past in influencing the budget such as was brought before the house at the last session. If the financial interests are successful in preventing from coming into Canada the imports that are necessary to pay for the British loan-and judging from experience I think under our present system they will be successful-Great Britain will face an adverse balance of payments. Britain, facing an adverse balance of payments, will find the shortage of United States dollars and Canadian dollars very difficult. She will try to increase her exports by any means possible, and there will be a long time of disequilibrium in the balance of payments.
In order to increase her exports Britain will be forced to depreciate her currency. This depreciation will encourage British exports to Canada; it will at the same time discourage Canadian exports to Britain. We saw in September, 1931, the conditions which faced Canada that year, and they faced her also the next year, after Great Britain had devaluated her currency. We saw that the products of Canada, sent to the markets of Great Britain and turned into pounds, brought fewer Canadian dollars to the producers of those products. In November, 1932, we saw the price of wheat on the Winnipeg grain exchange hit an all-time low of forty cents a bushel, basis No. 1 northern, Fort William, and the depression was certainly on. We saw few jobs in Canada. There was no effective demand for goods. Canadian boys by the thousand rode the rods. If we are not to have those conditions return we must take full cognizance of the situation which will face us after 1951. There is only one way whereby we can accept more British imports, and that is by having full employment in Canada, having everybody here who is willing and able to work, working and obtaining a decent wage or salary. They will then have the money to buy from Great Britain the imports which will add materially to the welfare of all our people.
There is another thing we shall be forced to do. I believe that never again in the future should the people of Canada acquiesce in the idea that the price they obtain for their products in Canadian dollars shall be governed entirely by the price paid for those products on the world market. Canadian farmers at this time need, shall we say, $1.55 a bushel for their wheat. At this time there is no real relation between anv so-called world market price and the price the farmers receive for their products. But our farmers are enjoying more prosperity than they did in 1932 when their prices were hooked up with world

prices. The price the farmer receives for his products should be such that out of an economy of full employment in Canada he shall receive his fair share of the national income; the same with the worker; the same with all classes of people. Surely never again do we want to hook our whole economy to a fluctuating world market price. If anything important is going on in the world to-day in the changes which all governments are making in their outlook respecting the industrial and financial life of their nations, it is that almost everywhere governments are deciding that they must have complete ownership and control of the banking system. If we are to have the full production and full employment which will be necessary to permit Canadians to use the goods which Britain will have to export, we must of necessity socialize the banks so that the government will have available to them at the cost of banking, which is very little, the Canadian dollars that are necessary to pay to the people of Canada as a reward for their labour.
I believe this measure which is before the house will serve a useful purpose to all the people of Canada. We see the government at this time cancelling a $425 million debt of Great Britain, at the same time that we are lending to Great Britain on favourable terms SI,250 million. Surely we shall never again hear in this house what a minister told us the other day, in talking about payments for social security for people who are unable to earn their living, that $100 million is a very large amount. Surely, if we can get $1,250 million to loan to Great Britain we can get $100 million to provide security to these people in Canada who through no fault of their own are disabled and cannot obtain jobs. Surely we shall not again have an answer from the government-or a talking out of a motion, which is even worse-that there is not available $100 million for irrigation in all of the area of western Canada. If the government intends to make the present system work at all, this loan makes it more imperative than ever that we shall have full production, full employment, adequate social security; and these measures, I submit, can be brought about only by socializing the banks, whereby we can make the currency available which is necessary to run the economy of Canada as it is best suited to the needs of the people of Canada.

Speaking upon this bill, I wish to say in the first place that I regard the credit of $1,250 million to Britain simply as an assur-

ance of employment in this country. It is neither more nor less than that. Without extending the credit we shall be poor, because our people will not be employed; if we extend the credit the reverse can be true.
Reference has been made in the debate, both on the resolution and on this motion for second reading, to what has been called good commercial practice. The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Maedonnell) spoke of the need a merchant sometimes found of extending credit in his own interest. In respect of this credit I think we can very well liken ourselves to a man of business who has had customers over a number of years who gave him a great deal of business, well-to-do customers who made up about forty per cent of his business, and then these customers became temporarily embarrassed and could not deal with him any longer on a cash basis. Paced with that prospect, any merchant if he were wise would know what to answer. He would certainly say to such customers that they could continue to obtain their needs from him without cash. He would know that if he could hold the business by granting credit he could carry on as before; he could keep his employees employed as before; he could, as they say, maintain his organization, and perhaps he could even expand it. Eventually he would be repaid in full; and altogether he could regard the situation as one which held foi him a good future. Incidentally-but only incidentally in the business view-he would be helping toward a less austere life the people who had been his good customers.
That is exactly our position at the present time; at least it is as near to an exact comparison as we can get in likening an individual's business to a nation's business. Such a comparison can never be quite exact, but I believe it is close enough in this case for us to begin to see clearly the nature of this proposition.
I wish to comment further on the employment and unemployment features which present themselves to me in the consideration of this bill; but before I do so I should like to deal with some of the criticisms that have been made. I noted the objections of the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin). He thinks this loan is for the grandeur and prestige of England. He looks on it as a prop for the central structure of an empire. This, to him, seems to be colonialism. I regard his approach as a grave mistake. The motives underlying the loan are purely economic and purely Canadian. I am not denying that there is altruism in the country, but the compelling motives are economic and Canadian.

What strikes me in listening to charges of subservience to England is that these excessive warnings tend to become ludicrous. I believe if that sort of thing is continued, then, when some real danger does arise, of a kind about which the hon. gentleman, as an elder statesman, might wish to warn us, his vibrant voice will be without authority at all owing to the fact that he has continually and for a long time been trying to make our flesh creep with scare talk about a bogey-man that does not really exist.

I should like to say a few words more about this "colonialism" charge, and I do not now refer particularly to the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres or to the hon. member for Temiscouata. But there do come from time to time innuendoes and hints, charges and statements from some hon. members that a great number of us who do not live in the lower province are not Canadians. We hear it every once in a while, or we hear suggestions of it.
Of course I realize how false the charge is. Speaking as I do with other Canadians across the country and with their representatives in this House of Commons, I see how wrong it is. I know that, so far as I am concerned, I am never moved by any considerations that are not purely Canadian. Although I see the incongruity of the charge, it does appear that some people are of the opinion that we who have not that great advantage of the two languages are not Canadians, that we look at all propositions first with the eyes of English and, second, with the eyes of Canadians. I tell the house, frankly, I get very tired of what it seems to me is a sort of frenzy of Canadianism. I think some of those hon. gentlemen who put forth that sort of criticism are sometimes very much like the Pharisee who spent a great deal of his time in thanking

God that he was not as other men. I remember hearing of a man of whom it was said that he used to go to the rain barrel and yell down into it, declaring his own virtues in order that they might be sounded back by echo into his ears; and to him this was as music. Such is the attitude of some bf those who would charge others with being non-Canadian. They smite their breasts extolling their own Canadianism. People will approach an economic question of this sort from different directions. Some will be more moved than others over the benefit that may be gained by some place remote from their own country, not because .they love their own country less, but because they think that from the point of view of their own country that gain which would help another country will be best in the long run for their own. I have no hesitation in saying that it has alwaj's been my view that the best way to help your own country is to help another country. I do not believe there is any doctrine as good in an economic sense as the golden rule. It is a fine rule ethically; but speaking quite coldly, it is a good rule in economics too. We shall do well, whenever we can to help another nation, because we have to deal with other nations. If we deal with them in the strength of economic health we can get the benefit of that health. If they are not in economic health we get the dis-benefit of their unhealthy condition. If I view the problem in this way that is not to say that I do not view it as a Canadian; it is not to be said that I view it as an Englander, or as a foreigner. Mine is a Canadian approach.
I sometimes think people who are inclined to make charges of un-Canadianism or less than 100 per cent Canadianism against some other people are really troubled by an inferiority complex which is unworthy of them. Sometimes it is called a persecution complex. If they have not such a complex there is danger of their being thought to be thus afflicted. One does not have to go around hunting Englishmen to spit in their faces in order to be a 100 per cent Canadian. That is not necessary at all. I am not denying that there may be a few people in the country who do not always view matters from a Canadian angle. There probably are some who still have a colonial mind but they are very few in number by now.
Hear, hear.

There are a few, but they are hardly worth noticing. One should not even waste the wind that is necessary

to say, "Hear, hear", over such people. For example, with respect to any virtue that a person may have, or with respect to any belief that he may have, it is not necessary to be blatant about it. So far as these few colonial people whom I have mentioned are concerned they are really a pathetic people. One should not upbraid them; one should not condemn them or abuse them in any way. No person has any right to do that at all.
This credit to Britain is simply for our own welfare and that is the way we ought to look at it. If we extend it we sell goods. If we do not extend it we do not sell goods. Selling goods means selling our work products. If we do not sell goods, we do not sell our work products and that means unemployment. This is a premium on a policy of insurance against unemployment. As a result of this loan we know Britain will spend a certain amount of money in a year. We can take any figure that we like for purposes of illustration. We can think of Britain spending $500 million in a year. That will do for illustration purposes at this moment, although it is quite probable that the purchases will be greater than that. How many hours of labour that will purchase it is hard to say. If the average rate for labour were fixed at $1 an hour it would mean 500 million hours of labour. It might be fair to say that the expenditure would give half a billion hours of work, because we can think of the rate as being fifty cents an hour. However. we have to remember that some of the labour that is bought has already been expended, and is in our country at the present time in the form of machines and other kinds of works. Anybody pursuing the idea of the value of British purchases upon Canadian employment can get much statistical data of interest. Statistical stories over the years tell us that whenever we have had a high level of employment it immediately followed a high level of export trade. Conversely, whenever we had a low level of employment it was consequent on a low level of export trade. For example, we reached the peak of our export volume pre-war in 1928. It was followed in 1929 by the highest level of employment and

the highest level of income. Again in 1932 we had the lowest level of export trade, and it was fpllowed in 1933 by the lowest level of employment and income.
Our export trade is largely British. Our net exports to Britain have been greatest by far in the ten years before the war. We sold to her in that period SI,647 million worth of goods more than we bought. That was the net. Incidentally our dealings with the United States were just the opposite, because we bought a billion dollars worth more than we sold. Let us consider for a moment what happens if $1,000,000 is spent on lumber products, for instance. Let us take as a unit of measurement 1,000 board feet of lumber. In my hand I have a graph which shows the amount of labour involved in the various products coming from a log containing that amount of lumber. Apparently the log itself represents one man's work for one day. In sulphite pulp it represents three days' work or, if it is exported, the measure becomes four days' work. If it is in newsprint it represents three days of labour, but if it is exported that figure becomes four days. If it is in bags or cartons the number shown here is nine days; if those products are exported, it becomes eleven days. So that one can follow upon this graph all the products that may result from the cutting down of a tree in the forest. From this we can get some idea of the exact results from the expenditure of $1,000,000 on lumber. That would represent approximately one million hours. In a 300-day year at eight hours a day a man would work 2,400 hours, so that it would take him 417 years to work enough hours at $1 an hour to use up that $1,000,000 or the same as 417 men for one year.
One can look at the industrial picture in this way, not only with respect to lumbering but with respect to every other industry. of $1,000,000. Of course, it is not only copper or lumber products that are to be bought; in all probability Britain will buy with these moneys the same sort of things she has bought in the past, when her purchases were very much diversified, and $1,000,000 is only a fraction of what will be spent.

Mr. Speaker, before the house rose at six o'clock I was giving some figures based upon a certain assumption as to the probable employment given by the expenditure of moneys from this loan by Great Britain in Canada. Varying the assumption somewhat, I have attempted to arrive in another way at an approximation of the employment content of these expenditures, assuming that half the proceeds of the loan will be spent in the purchase of non-agricultural products and not considering the length of time in which those purchases will occur.
In 1944 our national production excluding agriculture and excluding payments to the armed services, was registered at $9,110 million. That production was the result of the work of 3,280,000 people. It will be found that that represents an output of $2,770 per person. If we apply that factor to the expenditure of S625 million, one-half the loan, on non-agricultural goods we find that employment will be given to 200,000 persons for a full year.
As every person must realize, this employment will affect a great variety of people in all walks of life, the lumberjack in British Columbia, the miner in Quebec, the factory worker in Ontario, the dock worker in the maritimes, the manufacturer in Toronto and the wholesaler in Montreal. On the basis of four persons to a family, these expenditures will provide a livelihood for 800,000 people in this country for a full year.
I have said that this might very well be regarded as insurance against unemployment. Conversely, I could have said equally well that it is a subsidy for employment. It is a better sort of subsidy for employment than the subsidies for public works of which we sometimes hear. I am not decrying subsidies for public works when the need arises for them. I hope that never again will relief be necessary, but if it is I hope it will never be given except as payment for work. Public works are necessary at certain times, but a subsidy of this sort is of much greater value

in the creation of employment. This sort of expenditure means a diversification of the types of work created. Public works cannot employ such a wide variety of people as this type of expenditure. I think I can say with confidence that this sort of subsidy is the best subsidy we could have.
When an international loan is viewed in the way of creation of hours of employment I think we are justified in using an expression such as I have used, that it is a subsidy for employment or insurance against unemployment. Whether such expressions are apt or not, surely it is clear that such a loan is based firmly upon considerations of Canadian welfare. Some people may look upon this as aid to Britain. They have slight justification for taking that view.
It is certainly not a benevolence. We may not preen ourselves upon any altruism in the making of this loan. One may be tempted to say that it is just hard-boiled business, although I do not like the use of the expression "hard-boiled" with reference to it. We are not taking advantage of anybody. Undoubtedly the loan will be a great help to Britain, undoubtedly she is desperately in need of it and she wants it badly. We can be ve?y glad that it will be of help. Just the same it does not seem to me that altruism alone is sufficient ground for the Canadian parliament making this loan. If it were not in our own interests I do not think it would be possible for it to be made.
But I want to interject and say that I like to think of our actions as having some element of altruism and a consideration of other people's welfare in them, as well as a marked consideration of business principles. I said somewhat earlier that the doctrine of the golden rule not only is sound ethically, but is good economics as well. I cannot help being reminded that the whole cost of a war is not paid during the years of a war-the costs go on. During the last war I think we gave to the utmost of our capacity, or at least we approached the limit of our capacity to give. But unlike other nations, we do not have to pay a great cost of the war at the conclusion of the war. We are not paying like Great Britain is paying. The cost of a war is to be seen in the condition in which a country is left after the war. Unquestionably Britain has been left much poorer in 1916 than she was in 1939, but we cannot say that about ourselves. We are not poorer to-day than we were in 1939; we are better off.
Forgetting for a moment ordinary business principles, it does seem to me that one might
[Mr. Maybank.l
with justice favour this loan merely on the ground of fair play in order that we may continue to bear our own costs of the war. There are countries in the world to which we are indebted in a way that we can never repay. We are bound to think of the disaster that would have fallen upon us had Britain succumbed, a disaster from which none of us and none of our children would ever have recovered. We cannot say quite the same about certain other nations, but we are indebted to other nations such as, for example, Greece. I do not wish to make comparisons or to compile a list of those countries to which we are indebted, but there are many countries to which we owe much for the way in which they fought to avert the fate which would otherwise have overtaken the world. It is but fair when considering a measure of this sort to remember that these people are still paying the cost of the war, Great Britain probably in greater measure than any other, and they are all much worse off than they were in 1939. We are not in that position; we are better off. Therefore, while we should look at this loan as a business proposition, we should not overlook these other factors.
Not only is this loan in our own interests as a subsidy to employment; but we should remember that finally it will be paid not by us, but by Britain, so that the end result will be the subsidizing of employment in this country, not by Canadian dollars, for the subsidy will eventually be paid in pounds, shillings and pence.
There is one other thought which gives me a good deal of pleasure, and I wonder if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) may think it is a malicious pleasure. I wish briefly to express my unqualified support of the bill and to say how much I enjoyed the lucid manner in which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) presented the subject to the house. I have listened to arguments against, and for the bill. I have listened to what I consider rather unusual speeches. I listened to a few' members ns they spent thirty-nine minutes and forty seconds in pulling the bill to pieces and then telling the house in the last few seconds that they intended to support it.
I have listened also very carefully to the speech of the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), and I think he is entirely out of perspective when he talks about dealing with the sufferings of our own people in the terms he did in relation to the people of Europe at the present time. Regardless of the things that have to be done in Canada, the things that require to be done in the near future, I say that with the exception of those who have lost loved ones, and the men who went overseas, there is not a portion of the world to-day that is as fortunate as we are in Canada.
When the hon. member for Temiscouata was speaking, his arguments reminded me of the story of the church janitor who found the parson's notes od Monday morning as he was clearfing the church. He picked t,hem up. The parson had made various notations in his manuscript, and at one point he had, "Argument weak; raise your voice." At another point he had, "Argument very weak; wave your arms"; and at still another point he had, "Argument terribly weak; wave your arms and yell like hell".

Loan to United Kingdom
I think the arguments in favour of the bill have in some cases over-emphasized the economic advantages. I know we have to consider the matter from that point of view. But I am rising to express my support of the bill on the ground that we have a moral obligation to assist those who have suffered in the defence of democracy. We had to pool our resources to win the war, and I am quite sure that we shall have to pool our resources to win the peace. I look upon the bill, with its period of no interest and with its lower interest rates, as a step in the right direction. Because of that I support the bill unqualifiedly.

I do not expect to take a great deal of time, as the two previous speakers have indicated the importance of this bill, and if there are no other speakers I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that we can pass the bill to-night. I do wish, however, to make a few observations because I believe that there are important principles involved in this measure.
I have listened to arguments pro and con and I am not going to say that the argument is all on one side. There are arguments for both sides, although at the outset I wish to say that I support the bill. The bill provides for two separate amounts of money. One part of the bill provides for the cancellation of apy debt that the United Kingdom may ewe us in respect of the commonwealth air training plan; the other part provides for the extension of credits to the extent of one and a quarter billion dollars in order that Great Britain may purchase goods from Canada. The first item of $425,000,000, which is the United Kingdom's share in the commonwealth air training plan, will constitute, I take it, a direct gift to Great Britain, not from now on, because the gift has already been made.
May I suggest that we must have had to borrow the money in order to pay Great Britain's share in this commonwealth air training plan and our borrowings therefore have been used. They have been spent for the purpose of that plan. In other words, we have borne Britain's share of that plan to the extent of $425,000,000. This money has to be paid back. I cannot tell where this particular money came from because we have been raising billions of dollars throughout the war years by means of victory loans. I imagine that a large part of the $425 million is now owed' the chartered banks of Canada. I believe I am right, even though it may be a guess, that a good deal of the $425 million constitutes expanded credit which the banks now hold as a
debt against the Canadian people. It can be paid back only by taxation. The people of Canada should realize this. There is one painful cry that goes up from the people of Canada to-day, namely, the cry of the pain of over-burdening taxation.
It is all very well to talk about extending credits and cancelling debt, but the people of Canada should know that every time we cancel a foreign debt there is a corresponding debt here in Canada which has to be paid, and it can be paid only by taxation; of course, as the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hlymika) reminds me, under the present system. That is what we are operating under, the management of this system by the Liberal administration of this country. Suppose, instead of giving the loan to Britain we should ask the people of Canada whether they are ready to foot the bill to the tune of $425 million by taxation. If we did that it would put a little different complexion on this question in the minds of the people of Canada. I will make this observation. The government does not seem much alarmed at the cancellation and the eventual payment of debt to the tune of $425 million. That is strange to me, because a few years ago when we had plenty of goods for everyone in Canada and asked the government for a few paltry dollars they could not supply the money.

gentleman a question? How does the can- . cellation of $425 million of debt add to the taxes of the people of Canada if the debt is beyond the capacity of the debtor to pay?
That is a good admission.

I will answer, and I do not propose now to match my economic brains with those of the Minister of Finance; but I think he will agree that any debt that exists is a debt that is caused by the expansion of credits, and any expansion of credit is a debt to the banking institutions of Canada. To that extent it must be paid by the people of Canada.

It might have been incurred years ago, but it is still here and is perhaps a little bigger now by the addition of accrued interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has not answered the question.

I may not have answered the question to the satisfaction of the Minister of Finance, but that is my answer and it is satisfactory to me.
Loan to United, Kingdom

Let me ask the finance minister a question. Why is it that Canada can now provide $1,250 million of credit to Britain when she could not provide much less than that for the people of Canada a few years ago? I have paused, and the minister has not answered.
There are two ways of approaching the argument in respect of this loan. Many of the speakers in favour of the loan have spoken of it on the basis that it is good business. A second argument is that there is a moral obligation. I wish to ask hon. members if they think the extension of these credits to Britain to the extent of $1,250 million is good business? Let us look at that because a previous speaker said that there would be greater employment, greater production and greater export trade. It is true that for the time being there will be greater employment. But let us remember this, that greater employment here on goods to be exported means greater unemployment to the importing country. I know we are not living in normal times economically to-day. There is a disequilibrium in our economic set-up in these years because Of the war and so forth, but I am talking now of whether the loan is good business. Exports mean that you are exporting your unemployment. To the extent that export trade increases employment in one country, generally speaking it means corresponding unemployment in another country. I ask, is that good business? It may be for 'us and only for a time.
I come now to the matter of greater production. It will mean greater production, but let us remember that the greater production is to go out of. the country. What we are really doing is shipping our real wealth out of our own country. We may be provided with a certain amount of money through increased employment, but the real wealth is gone. I ask, is that good business? Perhaps some of the orthodox minds would say that it is. Some person will say that it is good business because it means greater exports. It just so happens that at the present time we need the goods. Is it good business to ship out the goods when we need them here? Let me follow that up. When a credit is paid by the importing country it is paid by that country importing goods. When Great Britain pays the money back she pays us by sending us goods. Therefore the position that we are placed in is that we are shipping out goods now when we need them, but we shall be taking them back when we do not need them.

Is the hon. member opposed to shipping them out now?
[Mr. Hansell.l

No. I suppose this is the crucial time, anyway, for Great Britain certainly needs them now. I am not talking against the bill; I do not want my hom friends to misunderstand me. What I am trying to make clear is that there are two ways of looking at it. One is from the point of view of whether or not it is good business; the other is whether there is a moral obligation. I am not supporting the bill because it is good business. I think it is the business of lunatics. I am supporting the bill because we have a moral obligation toward the people of Great Britain.
While we are talking about whether or not it is good business, let me dwell for a moment on this matter of inflation. Oh, how the cry used to go up some years ago when we wanted a few extra dollars. The same hon. gentlemen now sitting on the treasury benches replied, "Oh, that would be inflation." We dared not talk in terms of $100,000,000 without its being called inflation, but now here is $1,250 million. When we proposed a little extra money there were plenty of goods to correspond with any such increase, but the cry went up that it would be inflation, and we could not have that. Now, however, we can supply a billion and a quarter of money when we have no goods behind it. From the point of view of business it is not good business, because this will aggravate inflation, the very thing we want to prevent. I say, then, that from the point of view of whether or not it is good business, I do not believe it is. We have a shortage of goods here, perhaps more shortages than we know about. I went to buy a pair of socks to-day. Since the Minister of Finance asked me a question I should like to ask him where I can buy a pair of socks. I have darned the ones I have until I cannot darn them any more, darn it, and I should like to know where I can get socks.
The only reason remaining for the loan, as far as I can see, is from the moral aspect. The hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Matthews) has expressed it as adequately as anyone could in a few minutes. I too, have an aged mother there, and we feel very much concerned about this thing. The fact is that Great Britain has suffered; she has been in the front line alone throughout the war. Her real wealth is gone. Her machinery is worn out. The present scarcity in the United Kingdom is such that they are almost at the point of starvation; at least they are at the point where the government is now talking of rationing bread. This is so in spite of the fact that a few years ago we reduced our production of wheat and paid our farmers

not to grow it. That was the policy of the present government. If hon. members do not think this a lunatic policy I do not know what we can be thinking about. You see, the Lord was so good to us, but we thought he did not know his business. He sent us so much sunshine and so much rain that we had too much, so that the government went the Lord one better; they knew a little more. They said, "Well, we cannot very well reach up into the sky and turn off the rain. We cannot very well reach up and pull down the blind so that the sun will not shine, but we know what we can do. We can take this asinine financial system and pay our men not to produce, when the good Lord gives us the opportunity to do so." I did not like to say this when the legislation was brought down, but I feel like saying it now, that I had to choose between Gardiner and God.

I thank the Prime Minister for his motion, but I shall take only a minute or two. I was saying there was a time when we could have produced more, but the policy of the government was to pay people not to produce. Well, now the chickens are coming home to roost, and we have scarcity. That is the result of what I would call the blundering financial and agricultural policy of this administration.
There is one other point, with which the hon. member for Temiseouata (Mr. Pouliot) dealt just before he sat down. I believe he made the point that this bill would do more than anything else to promote communism in Canada. I believe that was an unfortunate observation. Personally I doubt whether he really meant what he said, but in any event he said it. The fact of the matter is that it is not the loan that will cause any trouble in respect of communism. It will be the financial policy of the country-and I am not talking about loans now but about the policy with respect to debt and taxation-that will do more than anything else to make people in Canada dissatisfied. I would say to the hon. member for Temiseouata and those hon. members from Quebec who haye spoken against the loan that I appreciate their position. They are fine men; they have convictions, but if I could leave one message with them to-night it would be that the democracies of the world must stand together. They must reciprocate one with the other in the common interest of all. If they do not do that I am afraid communism will take over. That is something to be considered. We must live together or we shall die separately.
Once' again I wish to emphasize-ahd I think I am speaking for my group, or in any event for some of them-that we support this bill on moral grounds. If we were in power, perhaps we would assist Great Britain even to a greater extent, but our financial policy would not be the one that the present government has. We support the bill because of a moral obligation and we trust, indeed we know that there will always be an England.
